title: Taxation Basics
summary: Learn how taxes work: principles and types of tax, personal income tax with bands and marginal rates, company tax and taxable profit, VAT mechanics, withholding and compliance, and the line between planning, avoidance and evasion.
audience: Students, employees, freelancers, small-business owners and junior accountants

lessons.title: Why we pay tax and how tax systems work

body.p: Taxes fund public services such as schools, clinics, roads, security and social grants. Governments also use taxes to influence behaviour, for example taxing tobacco or giving incentives for investment. A good tax system aims to be fair, simple, certain, efficient to collect and hard to avoid.

list: Direct taxes on income and wealth: personal income tax, company income tax, capital gains tax.
Indirect taxes on spending: value-added tax (VAT) or sales tax, excise duties on alcohol, tobacco and fuel, and customs duties on imports.
Payroll taxes and social contributions.
Property and local taxes.

body.p: A progressive tax takes a higher share from higher incomes (most income taxes). A proportional (flat) tax takes the same share. A regressive tax takes a larger share of income from poorer people; VAT can be regressive because poorer households spend more of their income, which is why basic foods are often exempt or zero-rated.

body.tip: Tax rates, bands and thresholds change, usually in each annual budget. Always check current figures with your country's revenue authority.

body.p: Most countries tax individuals on employment income, business profits, rent and investment income, using progressive bands. Employees usually pay through PAYE, deducted by the employer each month.

body.h: A worked example with illustrative bands

body.p: Suppose income up to 100 000 is taxed at 0%, income from 100 000 to 300 000 at 20%, and income above 300 000 at 30% (these are teaching figures, not any country's actual rates). On an income of 450 000: the first 100 000 is tax-free, the next 200 000 is taxed 40 000, and the remaining 150 000 is taxed 45 000, a total of 85 000.

list: Average (effective) rate = 85 000 / 450 000, about 18.9%.
Marginal rate = 30%: an extra 10 000 of income adds 3000 of tax.
Moving into a higher band only taxes the income above the band limit at the higher rate, not the whole income.
Deductions and reliefs (such as pension contributions, where allowed) reduce taxable income; tax credits or rebates reduce the tax itself.

body.tip: Keep payslips, tax certificates and receipts for deductions; you will need them for returns and any queries.

body.p: Companies pay income tax on taxable profit, which often differs from accounting profit. Sole traders and partners are usually taxed on business profits as personal income.

body.h: From accounting profit to taxable profit

body.p: Start with accounting profit, add back expenses the law does not allow (such as fines, some entertainment and accounting depreciation where tax allowances replace it), and subtract exempt income and tax allowances. Example: accounting profit 500 000, non-deductible expenses 20 000 and exempt dividend income 30 000 give taxable profit of 500 000 + 20 000 - 30 000 = 490 000. At a 27% rate (South Africa's company rate at the time of writing), tax is 132 300. Rates differ by country and sometimes by company size.

list: Capital allowances (wear-and-tear allowances) give tax relief for buying equipment over several years.
Losses can often be carried forward to reduce future taxable profits.
Small-business regimes, such as turnover taxes, simplify tax for small firms in several countries.
Companies pay provisional or instalment tax during the year in many systems.

body.tip: Record business expenses with proper invoices; undocumented expenses may be disallowed.

body.p: VAT is charged at each stage of production and distribution, but businesses reclaim the VAT on their purchases, so the tax is ultimately borne by the final consumer. Businesses above a turnover threshold must register.

A registered business sells goods for 200 000 (before VAT) at 15%, charging output VAT of 30 000. It bought supplies for 120 000 and paid input VAT of 18 000. It pays the tax authority 30 000 - 18 000 = 12 000. If input VAT is larger than output VAT, the business can usually claim a refund.

list: Standard-rated supplies: VAT at the normal rate.
Zero-rated supplies: VAT at 0%, but input VAT can still be reclaimed (often exports and some basic foods).
Exempt supplies: no VAT charged, and related input VAT cannot be reclaimed (often financial services, some education and health).
Valid tax invoices are needed to claim input VAT.

body.p: Excise duties add specific taxes on goods such as fuel, alcohol and tobacco; customs duties apply to imports according to their tariff classification.

body.tip: Keep VAT collected separate from business cash; it belongs to the revenue authority.

body.p: Withholding taxes collect tax at the source of a payment. Examples include PAYE on salaries, withholding on dividends, interest and royalties, and in some countries on payments to contractors. A 10% withholding tax on a 10 000 payment means the payer sends 1000 to the tax authority and pays 9000 to the recipient, who may credit the 1000 against their final tax.

list: Register with the revenue authority and obtain a tax identification number.
File returns and pay on time, usually through online systems.
Keep records for the legally required period, often five years or more.
Respond promptly to queries and audits.
Use a tax calendar listing every deadline.

body.p: Late filing and late payment attract penalties and interest, and serious non-compliance can lead to prosecution. Many revenue authorities offer voluntary disclosure programmes that reduce penalties for those who correct past mistakes before being caught.

body.tip: If you cannot pay in full, contact the revenue authority before the deadline to discuss payment arrangements; ignoring it makes things worse.

body.p: Taxpayers may arrange their affairs to pay no more tax than the law requires. The distinction between acceptable and unacceptable behaviour matters:

list: Tax planning: using reliefs as the law intends, such as contributing to a pension or claiming allowances for new equipment.
Aggressive tax avoidance: artificial arrangements that follow the letter but not the purpose of the law. Many countries have general anti-avoidance rules to defeat them.
Tax evasion: illegally hiding income or inventing expenses. It is a crime.
Double taxation agreements between countries prevent the same income being taxed twice and allocate taxing rights.
Transfer pricing rules require transactions between related companies in different countries to be priced as if between independent parties (the arm's-length principle).
Base erosion and profit shifting by multinationals costs developing countries significant revenue; international initiatives, including a global minimum tax for large groups, aim to reduce it.

body.tip: Professional advice is worthwhile for complex situations, but you remain responsible for your own tax returns.
